clinicalPearls: A common cause of early-infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, with seizures often beginning in the neonatal period or early infancy
Seizure types are varied and may include epileptic spasms with a burst-suppression or hypsarrhythmia EEG (Ohtahara or West syndrome patterns)
Some individuals have significant developmental impairment with little or no epilepsy, so the disorder spans an encephalopathy-with-or-without-seizures spectrum
Prominent features include hypotonia, movement disorders such as tremor, dystonia and ataxia, and later autistic behaviours
Caused by heterozygous loss-of-function or dominant-negative variants in STXBP1 (Munc18-1), usually de novo and autosomal dominant
Seizures may respond well to certain antiseizure medications even when development remains severely affected
Brain MRI is frequently normal or shows only non-specific findings
reference.pathophysiology: STXBP1 encodes Munc18-1, a syntaxin-binding protein essential for assembly of the SNARE complex that mediates synaptic vesicle docking and calcium-triggered neurotransmitter release. Heterozygous loss-of-function or dominant-negative variants reduce functional protein through haploinsufficiency and, in some cases, aggregation of misfolded protein, impairing synaptic transmission across excitatory and inhibitory networks. The resulting disturbance of neurotransmission produces cortical hyperexcitability and abnormal circuit function, manifesting as early epileptic encephalopathy, movement disorder and intellectual disability. The developmental impairment can be substantial even when seizures are controlled, reflecting the protein's ongoing role in synaptic function.
additionalDifferentials: KCNQ2 or SCN2A neonatal epileptic encephalopathy
Ohtahara and West syndromes of other causes
Pyridoxine-dependent and other treatable metabolic epilepsies
additionalInvestigations: EEG to identify burst-suppression, hypsarrhythmia or other epileptiform patterns
Brain MRI to exclude structural or acquired causes
Metabolic screen including a trial addressing treatable causes such as pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy
Chromosomal microarray and STXBP1-inclusive gene panel or exome sequencing
redFlags: Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have moderate to severe intellectual disability regardless of seizure control, though epilepsy can improve or remit over time in some. Outcome is variable across the spectrum, and management is supportive with attention to seizures, movement disorder and development.
pitfalls: Assuming controlling the seizures will normalise development
Not considering STXBP1 in developmental impairment without epilepsy
Omitting a trial for treatable metabolic epilepsies before concluding the diagnosis
Interpreting a normal MRI as excluding a genetic encephalopathy
references: GeneReviews: STXBP1 Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy
management: Antiseizure medication tailored to seizure type and EEG pattern, with ACTH or vigabatrin considered for epileptic spasms and a West syndrome pattern
Trial treatable-cause therapy such as pyridoxine and complete a metabolic screen before attributing the picture solely to STXBP1
Manage the movement disorder (tremor, dystonia, ataxia) and hypotonia with physiotherapy and targeted agents
Developmental support with early intervention, occupational and speech therapy, and communication aids for intellectual disability and autistic features
Confirm the diagnosis with an STXBP1-inclusive gene panel or exome sequencing and refer to clinical genetics
Genetic counselling noting variants are usually de novo with a generally low recurrence risk, while discussing the possibility of parental germline mosaicism
Multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental care, escalating for status epilepticus or developmental regression
